column4: The command وَدَعْ أَذَاهُمْ uses the section's و د ع root but makes their harm, rather than the Prophet, what is left; the same ayah tells him to entrust himself to Allah as Trustee.
The descending messengers explain an apparent interval by saying they descend only at the Lord's command and وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّا, directly excluding forgetful abandonment by “your Lord.”
To two frightened messengers Allah says إِنَّنِي مَعَكُمَا أَسْمَعُ وَأَرَى, turning feared exposure before Pharaoh into heard, seen companionship.
مُسْتَقَرَّهَا وَمُسْتَوْدَعَهَا directly joins each creature's settled place and deposited place under Allah's knowledge, while its provision remains His charge.
مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمُسْتَوْدَعٌ applies the section's deposit-and-abode pair to human generation from one soul.
فَآوَاكُمْ says Allah sheltered a small, vulnerable community that feared being snatched away, then strengthened and provided for it.
The youths' withdrawal from their people becomes refuge rather than abandonment: they are told to take shelter in the cave so their Lord will spread mercy and prepare ease.
Moses' mother is told to cast her infant into the river without fear or grief because Allah promises to return him; relinquishing the child becomes divine safekeeping.
The infant is placed in a chest and cast into the river, yet the command ends with his being formed عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي, a literal deposit kept under divine sight.
فَرَدَدْنَاهُ إِلَىٰ أُمِّهِ completes the river scene: the child entrusted beyond his mother's reach is returned so her eye may be comforted and she may know the promise true.
Joseph tells the people to leave harvested grain فِي سُنبُلِهِ, in its own enclosing ear, so “leaving” the provision is precisely how it is preserved.
The hard years consume the stored harvest except a little مِمَّا تُحْصِنُونَ; it states the protective result of the leaving-in-the-ear act in 12:47.
The Ark contains tranquility from the Lord and a remnant مِمَّا تَرَكَ آلُ مُوسَىٰ وَآلُ هَارُونَ; what a family leaves is borne and preserved rather than discarded.
A wall conceals treasure belonging to two orphans until maturity, making the Lord's unseen protection of an orphaned deposit the opposite of neglected care.
كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ names everything that passes away, supplying the departing half of the section's leaving-and-remaining relation completed in 55:27.
وَيَبْقَىٰ وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ places “your Lord” with what remains after all else perishes, giving Qur'anic force to the source dictionary's abiding sense beside رَبّ.
مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ اللَّهِ بَاقٍ states the image's distinction exactly: what is held by people runs out, while what is with Allah remains.
كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ gives the same ultimate boundary between what departs and the One who does not.
Lot says إِنِّي لِعَمَلِكُم مِّنَ الْقَالِينَ: the section's ق ل ي root is actual detestation here, directed at a people's deed, whereas 93:3 denies that the Lord treats the Prophet so.
The only other عَيْلَة names feared poverty and immediately promises فَسَوْفَ يُغْنِيكُمُ اللَّهُ, bringing the section's ع ي ل and غ ن ي words together as need reversed by divine sufficiency.
وَأَنَّهُ هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ attributes enrichment and lasting provision to Allah, directly paralleling فَأَغْنَىٰ.
وَإِن يَتَفَرَّقَا يُغْنِ اللَّهُ كُلًّا makes separation itself the setting in which Allah enriches both parties, meeting the section's departure and sufficiency in one claim.
كَأَن لَّمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا uses غ ن ي in the source dictionary's dwelling sense: the destroyed deniers are as though they had never remained in their homes.
كَأَن لَّمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا says Thamud's settled presence vanished as though they had never dwelt there, exposing how a dwelling can fail to remain.
Madyan too becomes كَأَن لَّمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا, another direct Qur'anic occurrence of the section's secondary غ ن ي sense of long residence.
كَأَن لَّمْ تَغْنَ بِالْأَمْسِ likens worldly growth cut down overnight to something that had not flourished or remained the day before.
Zakaria's plea رَبِّ لَا تَذَرْنِي فَرْدًا directly asks his Lord not to leave him solitary.
Allah answers 21:89 by granting Yahya and making his wife fit, replacing feared solitary abandonment with a household and divine response.
When the Prophet has been expelled and is one of two in the cave, لَا تَحْزَنْ إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَنَا and the descending tranquility stage divine companionship at the sharpest human leaving.
With the sea ahead and Pharaoh behind, Moses answers his companions' fear with كَلَّا إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ, confidence that his Lord has not left him.
The Prophet is told to endure his Lord's judgment because فَإِنَّكَ بِأَعْيُنِنَا, an explicit assurance of watchful keeping.
أَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِكَافٍ عَبْدَهُ reassures the threatened servant that Allah is sufficient for him while others try to frighten him.
In a moment of household opposition, the ayah declares Allah the Prophet's protector, followed by Gabriel, righteous believers, and angels as supporters.
يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ حَسْبُكَ اللَّهُ tells the Prophet that Allah is sufficient for him and joins believing followers to that support.
As Jacob must release another son to his brothers, فَاللَّهُ خَيْرٌ حَافِظًا makes Allah the better keeper of the one being entrusted away from home.
Jacob sends the son only after a binding pledge and ends اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ مَا نَقُولُ وَكِيلٌ, placing the risky departure under divine trusteeship.
Mary is accepted, caused to grow well, and placed in Zakaria's care; recurring provision in her sanctuary shows a child entrusted to both human and divine keeping.
The casting of pens decides أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ, making the choice of a guardian for the young Mary the ayah's central act.
A brother proposes putting Joseph in the hidden depth of a well so a caravan will pick him up, a calculated scene of leaving a child behind.
When Joseph is actually placed in the well, revelation reaches him there and promises a future reckoning, showing divine address continuing inside human abandonment.
After the well and sale, Joseph is given an honored lodging and possible adoption in Egypt; shelter answers the brothers' act of disposal.
آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ uses the section's sheltering verb for Joseph drawing his brother to himself after the family's long separation.
آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ uses the same verb for Joseph receiving his parents, so the root marks reunion and taking-in rather than departure.
Abraham says he has settled part of his offspring in an uncultivated valley and asks their Lord to draw hearts and provide fruit, a family left in divine care rather than discarded.
Noah's son says سَآوِي إِلَىٰ جَبَلٍ, but the mountain cannot protect him and the wave separates them; the ayah distinguishes false refuge from the mercy that truly shelters.
وَآوَيْنَاهُمَا إِلَىٰ رَبْوَةٍ ذَاتِ قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ joins divine sheltering of Mary and Jesus to a secure place of settlement and provision.
The breaker of dawn makes night سَكَنًا, directly pairing morning's emergence with the night's repose behind the section's oath.
Allah makes the night لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and the day visible, stating the night's divinely given stillness.
The ayah again says Allah made night so people may rest in it and day to give sight, the same night-as-repose relation.
From His mercy Allah gives both night for rest and day for seeking bounty, making stillness and provision alternating forms of care.
Allah makes night لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and day seeing, another direct formulation of the settled-night image.
Floodwater carries passing foam while مَا يَنفَعُ النَّاسَ فَيَمْكُثُ فِي الْأَرْضِ; the ayah makes vanishing and remaining visible in one scene.
إِنَّمَا هَذِهِ الْحَيَاةُ الدُّنْيَا مَتَاعٌ وَإِنَّ الْآخِرَةَ هِيَ دَارُ الْقَرَارِ names the near life as passing use and the hereafter as the abiding home.
Worldly life is rain-grown vegetation that becomes dry debris scattered by winds, a concrete image of what does not stay.
Beside 18:45's scattered growth, الْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ are better with the Lord, supplying what remains.
بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا identifies the human preference for what is nearer and passing.
وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ supplies the enduring counterpart to 87:16 and closely matches the surah's wider better-later horizon.
The disbelievers threaten their messengers with expulsion from the land; the Lord answers the threatened departure with a promise to destroy the wrongdoers.
وَلَنُسْكِنَنَّكُمُ الْأَرْضَ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ completes 14:13 by replacing threatened expulsion with settlement granted by the Lord.
The Prophet's opponents nearly drive him from the land, yet the ayah says they themselves would remain after him only briefly.
The plot to confine, kill, or expel the Prophet is set against Allah's counter-plan, showing human attempts to remove him held within divine governance.
The three “left behind” find no refuge from Allah except in Him; His turning toward them converts social and inward estrangement into restored relation.
وَلَا تَطْرُدِ الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُم forbids the Prophet to drive away vulnerable worshippers, using the very expulsion action named in the source explanation of قَلَىٰ.
Noah says وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا, refusing the elite's demand that he expel the believers who have joined him.
Noah asks who could help him against Allah if he drove the believers away, making abandonment of the vulnerable a breach of divine protection.
وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ repeats a messenger's refusal to drive believers away, directly reversing the source dictionary's driving scene.
The Prophet is told to keep himself patiently with those who call their Lord and not let his eyes pass beyond them, the positive act opposed to driving them away.
A released prisoner forgets Joseph, so فَلَبِثَ فِي السِّجْنِ بِضْعَ سِنِينَ; human forgetting leaves him to remain confined, unlike the Lord who does not forget.
Moses says his Lord's knowledge is in a record and لَا يَضِلُّ رَبِّي وَلَا يَنسَىٰ, another explicit denial of divine forgetting.
وَاللَّهُ مَعَكُمْ وَلَن يَتِرَكُمْ أَعْمَالَكُمْ joins divine companionship to a promise that believers' deeds will not be deprived of their due.
وَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى الْحَيِّ الَّذِي لَا يَمُوتُ tells the Prophet to entrust himself to the One whose life never departs.
فَإِنْ أَمِنَ بَعْضُكُم بَعْضًا فَلْيُؤَدِّ الَّذِي اؤْتُمِنَ أَمَانَتَهُ describes a deposit entrusted to another and the keeper's duty to return it.
Allah commands that trusts be rendered to their owners, stating the obligation created when something is left in another's keeping.
Guardians test orphans until maturity and then deliver their property to them, turning temporary custody into faithful preservation rather than appropriation.
A human beginning is placed as a drop فِي قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ, a secure receptacle that holds what has been deposited for development.
فَجَعَلْنَاهُ فِي قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ repeats the image of vulnerable life placed and kept in a secure lodging.
The Lord who feeds against hunger and grants safety against fear supplies the compact positive answer to need and exposure.
The cloud shades Israel while manna and quails are sent, joining the source dictionary's cloud image to sustained shelter and provision.
Allah shades the tribes with cloud and sends manna and quails, again making a cloud an enduring cover linked to care.
إِن يَنصُرْكُمُ اللَّهُ فَلَا غَالِبَ لَكُمْ is set against the explicit counterfactual وَإِن يَخْذُلْكُمْ; it names divine forsaking only to show that no other support could replace Him.
أَيَحْسَبُ الْإِنسَانُ أَن يُتْرَكَ سُدًى rejects the idea that a human is left unattended or without purpose, a general boundary around abandonment.
فَذَٰلِكَ الَّذِي يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ stages an orphan being forcefully repelled; its root is distinct from و د ع, but its action combines the section's driven-away and neglected-orphan images.
بَل لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ names failure to honor the orphan, the neglect from which the section derives the name يَتِيم.
The ban on betraying trusts marks the moral opposite of receiving something for faithful safekeeping.
فَالْيَوْمَ نَنسَاهُمْ is judicial abandonment in response to their forgetting the meeting, contrasting with 19:64's denial that the Lord is cognitively forgetful.
نَسُوا اللَّهَ فَنَسِيَهُمْ presents reciprocal punitive abandonment of hypocrites, defining a judgment boundary rather than ordinary forgetfulness.
The one who forgot Allah's signs is told وَكَذَٰلِكَ الْيَوْمَ تُنسَىٰ, a deliberate being-left-out in judgment that sharpens the positive assurance to the Prophet.
إِنَّا نَسِينَاكُمْ answers people's forgetting of the meeting with punitive abandonment, a specific reversal of divine remembrance and care.
الْيَوْمَ نَنسَاكُمْ repeats the judgment formula for those who forgot their meeting, showing where “not forgotten” no longer applies as relational favor.
وَاللَّيْلِ إِذْ أَدْبَرَ swears by night as it retreats, a direct moving-away counterpart to the night when it settles in 93:2.
وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَسْرِ depicts night journeying on, reversing the source section's night that becomes still and lasts.
وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا عَسْعَسَ presents night at a transition of approach or retreat, illuminating by contrast the unambiguous stillness stressed in the section.
Allah drives clouds, joins them, and makes them a mass before rain descends; the source dictionary's lingering cloud is here mobile and gathered under command.
Winds carry a heavy cloud and Allah drives it to dead land, so the cloud moves away yet its movement becomes delivery of life rather than expulsion.
The bad word is uprooted and has مِن قَرَارٍ no stability, the exact opposite of a protected or abiding placement.
A town once secure and amply provided is made to taste hunger and fear after ingratitude, reversing the shelter-and-provision pattern.
عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ supplies the turning-away act; 80:2 identifies the vulnerable blind man from whom the turn occurs.
The blind man comes to the Prophet, completing the encounter in which 80:1 stages relational withdrawal rather than reception.
أَمَّا مَنِ اسْتَغْنَىٰ uses غ ن ي for one who deems himself self-sufficient; attention goes toward him while the seeking man is neglected.
فَأَنتَ عَنْهُ تَلَهَّىٰ identifies inattention to the one who came striving and fearing in 80:8-9, a direct instance of overlooked care.
Those who consume orphan property turn a protected charge into self-enrichment, the betrayal opposite to sheltering one whose care is easily neglected.
The Messenger complains يَا رَبِّ that his people took this Qur'an مَهْجُورًا; human abandonment of the message stands against the Lord's non-abandonment of the Messenger.
وَاهْجُرْهُمْ هَجْرًا جَمِيلًا commands the Prophet to withdraw graciously from hostile speakers, using the very هجر wording by which the source dictionary explains severed farewell.
Abraham's father threatens stoning and orders وَاهْجُرْنِي مَلِيًّا, making familial expulsion the human rupture that the following ayat answer.
The brothers' lie says they left Joseph beside their belongings while they raced; even as fabricated speech, it precisely pictures a person left behind and exposed.
At Uhud the believers climb away without looking back while the Messenger calls from behind, staging human companions leaving the Prophet in danger.
Those who يَقْطَعُونَ مَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ أَن يُوصَلَ enact the severing that the source gloss says the Lord did not do.
Breaking Allah's covenant and cutting what He commanded joined repeats the relational rupture excluded from the Lord-Prophet bond.
وَتُقَطِّعُوا أَرْحَامَكُمْ makes severing kinship a condemned human act, clarifying the social force of a bond being cut.
Those who join what Allah commanded to be joined supply the positive relation opposite the source explanation's “he did not cut the bond.”
A good word is a good tree with a firm root, a living picture of what is made stable and continues to give.
The Prophet is told not to strain his eyes toward temporary worldly splendor because his Lord's provision is better and more enduring.
Worldly gifts are temporary enjoyment, while what is with Allah is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, another explicit passing-versus-abiding statement.
Worldly life is vegetation that pleases, yellows, and becomes debris; its staged decay makes the instability of present possession visible.
The counterfactual of night made perpetual asks who could bring light, placing permanence itself under the Lord's control.
The counterfactual of day made perpetual asks who could bring a night in which people rest, clarifying that settled night is a continuing gift rather than neglect.
If Allah stills the wind, ships remain رَوَاكِدَ on the sea, a non-night scene that nevertheless joins cessation to continued stillness.
Winds raise and spread clouds, then rain emerges; against the source dictionary's cloud that stays, this cloud's movement is the means of provision.
Allah sends winds that raise a cloud and drives it to dead land, another mobile-cloud reversal whose destination restores life.
Garments protect people from heat and violence, reversing the source dictionary example's direction: there the garment itself is put into a cover that protects it.
Permanent houses and light tents for travel show dwelling and departure as complementary provisions rather than abandonment.
One who leaves home migrating finds many places of refuge and abundance, and even death on the road leaves the reward secured with Allah.
The emigrants are expelled from homes and property, supplying the forced departure to which the settled hosts of 59:9 respond.
Those who settled in the Home love the emigrants who come to them and prefer them despite need, turning one group's displacement into another group's reception.
Those who migrate after wrong will be given a good worldly lodging by Allah, so departure under pressure leads to divinely granted settlement.
After the expulsion warning in 17:76, the unchanged divine way with earlier messengers says such removal cannot displace the Lord's enduring pattern.
A caravan draws Joseph from the well and hides him as merchandise; it ends literal abandonment while exposing him to another kind of concealment and loss of kin.
The former prisoner remembers Joseph after a long interval, ending the human forgetting that had left him confined in 12:42.
The youths أَوَى الْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ and ask their Lord for mercy and right guidance, the voluntary act of joining a refuge.
Allah seals the youths' hearing in the cave for counted years, making the refuge a place of sustained protected stillness.
The sun's course avoids the sleepers while they lie in an opening of the cave, detailing how their chosen refuge becomes a protected environment.
The sleepers are turned right and left while their dog guards the entrance, showing their hidden bodies actively preserved during the long stay.
Noah builds the ark بِأَعْيُنِنَا وَوَحْيِنَا, making the vessel that will keep its passengers a work under divine sight.
The ark sails بِأَعْيُنِنَا as recompense for the rejected Noah, another scene of a threatened servant and his charge preserved under divine watching.
A person seeking protection must be granted refuge and then conveyed to a place of safety, defining shelter as custody that ends in secure delivery.
Whoever entrusts himself to Allah finds Him sufficient; the same ayah says every matter has a divinely set measure.
When people warn believers that forces have gathered, they answer حَسْبُنَا اللَّهُ وَنِعْمَ الْوَكِيلُ, placing threatened lives in the best Trustee's care.
Giving orphans their property back and not consuming it with one's own defines the faithful handling of what belongs to a vulnerable ward.
Reform of orphans' affairs is called best and living together makes them brothers, replacing distance and neglected care with a household relation.
The command not to approach orphan property except in the best way until maturity treats it as a protected deposit.
The same boundary around orphan property lasts until maturity and is joined to fulfillment of the covenant, making guardianship accountable.
Those who fear leaving weak offspring behind are told to act justly, directly naming the anxiety that departure will expose dependent children.
Feeding an orphan despite love of the food supplies a concrete act of care for the one the section says is commonly overlooked.
Feeding an orphan of near kin on a day of hunger joins family attachment to material care rather than neglect.
Allah says He sent the Reminder and will guard it, a textual instance of something given forth yet continuously preserved.
بَلْ هُوَ قُرْآنٌ مَّجِيدٌ names the precious thing whose protected enclosure is specified in 85:22.
فِي لَوْحٍ مَّحْفُوظٍ places the Qur'an in a guarded tablet, paralleling the source dictionary's object kept inside a protective case.
After expulsion from the garden, earth is made a settlement and provision for a time, combining forced departure with a temporary abode.
The garden fall likewise ends with فِي الْأَرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَىٰ حِينٍ, a bounded replacement dwelling after removal.
Destroyed settlements become dwellings scarcely inhabited after their people, and Allah remains the inheritor; residence, departure, and what remains are held together.
فَاذْكُرُونِي أَذْكُرْكُمْ gives remembrance as a reciprocal divine-human relation, the positive counterpart to being forgotten or left out.
Allah says فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ and answers the caller, a direct statement of responsive nearness that rules out inattentive distance.
At Hunayn the believers' numbers do not avail them and they turn away, creating the abandonment-like battlefield reversal answered in 9:26.
Allah then sends tranquility upon His Messenger and believers and unseen forces, restoring support after the flight in 9:25.
Abraham withdraws from his people and their objects of worship while continuing to call on his Lord, so human separation does not become separation from God.
When Abraham withdraws, Allah grants him Isaac and Jacob and makes them prophets, replacing lost family company with a divinely given family.
The people are likened to startled donkeys; this recalls the source dictionary's wild-ass scene, though here the animals are the fleeing group rather than a male driving females.
فَرَّتْ مِن قَسْوَرَةٍ completes 74:50 with flight from a pursuer; the link to the source's driven herd is concrete but the agent and direction differ.
The panting chargers recall the source dictionary's horse released into open country, though the ayah depicts running and does not itself say the horses were abandoned or let loose.
